messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kalani is a 53-year-old photographer whose work, once celebrated for its intimate portraiture, has become a source of profound fear. It has been eighteen months since his three-week captivity while on assignment, and the world no longer feels like a place he can navigate with his camera. He was taken by a local militia and held in a small, windowless room, often bound to a chair. His captors were unpredictable, their moods shifting without warning. Kalani learned that a sudden movement—a quick turn of the head, a hand reaching for a belt—was often the only prelude to violence or intimidation. Confined and powerless, his survival depended on his ability to watch, to anticipate, to read the kinetic language of his guards. He spent every waking moment cataloging these threats, a practice that has followed him home.

In the months after his release, the relief he expected never arrived. Instead, the heightened state of alert he had adopted in that room became his new baseline. His body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, a low-frequency hum of anxiety that never ceases. He finds himself startled by the most innocuous actions; a waiter approaching his table too quickly or a pedestrian changing direction can put him immediately on guard. He has come to believe that the world is filled with hidden dangers and that only his constant watchfulness keeps him safe. This pervasive sense of threat has reshaped his daily existence, dictating his movements and interactions with a rigid, fearful logic.

This feeling of being under siege has led Kalani to develop a series of elaborate safety rituals. Because he is so attuned to the threat in sudden movements, he cannot enter a new space without first methodically planning an escape route. At his studio, at a café, or even at a friend's home, he immediately identifies all exits, mentally rehearsing his path out. When he does sit, he always chooses a seat based on how safe or protected he feels, typically in a corner with his back to a solid wall, allowing him an unobstructed view of the room's entrance. He is constantly vigilant for dangerous people, his gaze sweeping over faces in a crowd, searching for any sign of aggression. He frequently asks his wife for confirmation, whispering, "Does that guy over there seem okay to you?" seeking a reassurance that provides only fleeting comfort.

These very strategies, however, have become the architecture of his prison. The constant act of planning an escape route and seeking a safe seat serves as a relentless confirmation of his belief that an attack is imminent, which in turn keeps his body on high alert. His hypervigilance towards people makes him misinterpret neutral social cues as threatening, causing a jolt of fear when a stranger reaches into a pocket or makes an unexpected gesture. This locks him into a feedback loop of anxiety; the more he scans for danger, the more potential threats he perceives, which reinforces his need to scan. His reassurance seeking has also begun to strain his marriage, as his wife’s affirmations that he is okay are immediately erased by his underlying conviction that he is not, perpetuating his sense of being unable to trust his own judgment about safety.

His work, the core of his identity, has suffered most. A photographer needs to move freely, to be present with their subjects, to be open to the unexpected. For Kalani, this is now impossible. During a recent corporate headshot session, the client adjusted his tie with a quick movement, and Kalani flinched so visibly that the shoot had to be paused. He has started turning down assignments that require travel or shooting in public spaces. He finally sought help after refusing a major commission in Europe, a job that would have once been a career highlight. The thought of navigating airports, hotels, and unfamiliar city streets was overwhelming. "I used to look through my lens and see a person's story," he said in his first session. "Now I just see a collection of potential movements, and I'm waiting for the one that's going to hurt me."
